summary: A proposed Remote Job Entry protocol for submitting batch jobs from one network host to another. A user connects by Telnet to a special logger for control, and the server then uses FTP to fetch the job input and deliver the output. It was drafted by Chuck Holland and invited comment. It was replaced by RFC 407.

plainLanguage.summary: You hand a big job to a faraway computer. It picks up the instructions, does the work, and sends back the printed results, just like dropping off and collecting laundry.

questions: how did arpanet rje work with telnet and ftp
subtitle: A 1972 proposal for submitting batch jobs to another network host using Telnet for control and FTP for files.

tldr.problem: Users needed a standard way to run a batch job on a remote host and get its output delivered elsewhere.
tldr.mechanism: The user opens a Telnet control connection to a special RJE logger and sends text commands. The server then uses FTP to fetch the job input and deliver the output.
tldr.outcome: This proposal was obsoleted by RFC 407.

today: RFC 360 was obsoleted by RFC 407, so it is an early proposal rather than the final RJE specification.

sections.title: How Remote Job Entry Works
sections.content:
Remote job entry lets a user at one location cause a batch job to run at another. The user talks to the server over a Telnet control connection to a special standardized logger (socket 5, not socket 1). The server then uses the File Transfer Protocol to retrieve the job-input file and deliver the output files.

Users may be a person at a terminal on a TIP or any host, or an RJE user process on another host. Commands and replies are designed to suit both.
sections.plainLanguage: You tell the faraway computer what to do by typing messages. It then fetches your files itself and sends the results where you asked.

sections.title: Commands Over Telnet
sections.content:
Each command is one line ending in crlf. Recognized words are case-insensitive. The first command on a new connection must be USER, followed by PASS if a password is needed. BYE ends the session.

INPUT (or INPATH) names where to fetch the job from, either a host and socket or a host and file. OUT says what to do with each output file: transmit then discard by default, (H) hold, (S) transmit and save, or (D) discard. CHANGE alters it later. STATUS, CANCEL, ALTER and OP inspect or steer a job, and RESTART, RECOVER, BACK, SKIP, ABORT and HOLD control output in transmission.

Some commands can also appear as NET control cards at the front of the input file, where they take precedence for that job.
sections.plainLanguage: You type short commands like a menu order: who you are, where your job is, and where the answers should go.

sections.title: Using FTP for Files
sections.content:
For most non-TIP files the server calls its local FTP user process, which opens a new FTP connection for each file with 8-bit bytesize. Input uses Retrieve and output uses Append (with create). The FTP type, structure and mode depend on direction and the transmission and code options the user chose.

On output in Hasp form the server sends Restart-markers periodically, such as every 100 lines or so. If a transfer for an (S) file fails, the file is held, and the user can issue RECOVER to restart from the last marker.
sections.plainLanguage: The faraway computer uses a separate delivery truck for each file, and remembers how far the truck got in case it breaks down.

sections.title: Reply Codes
sections.content:
Every action is answered with a three-digit code, a blank and a text explanation, so both people and programs can read it. The first digit gives the type: 000 informative, 100 status reply, 200 positive acknowledgement, 300 incomplete information, 400 unsuccessful, 500 incorrect or illegal command; 600 to 900 are reserved.

The second digit gives the subject: for example x30 is primary access (log-on), x50 FTP results and x60 RJE results.
sections.plainLanguage: After each command the server answers with a number. The first digit tells you quickly if it went well or badly.

items.label: Status reply
items.desc: Reply to a specific status inquiry.

items.label: Positive acknowledgement
items.desc: Command accepted; 200 is a general ok.

items.label: Incomplete
items.desc: More information is needed to proceed.

items.label: Unsuccessful
items.desc: Correct request that could not be completed.
